title: An Ancient Cousin and a Second Emigrant

lessons.title: rot — "red"
lessons.gloss: red — the third colour, and the one humans name first after black and white

segments.text: You have black and white. The next colour is not a matter of taste — languages the world over reach for the same one third.
rot — "red."
Three letters, one syllable, and very close to the English word underneath the spelling.
long-o — the o is long, the vowel of English road, not the short o of rot. The German word does not rhyme with the English word spelled the same way.
d-t-final — the closing t is crisp and fully released: roht.

If a language has only two colour words, they are dark and light. If it has a third, it is red — before green, before blue, before yellow. That holds across unrelated families on every continent, which is why schwarz, weiß and rot are the three this chapter and the last one reach for first.
Blood and fire are the guess most people make, and it may be right; what is certain is the order, not the reason.

segments.instruction: the three in order — "schwarz, weiß, rot"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three in order — "schwarz, weiß, rot"]

segments.instruction: the warning — "rot does not rhyme with English rot"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the warning — "rot does not rhyme with English *rot*"]

segments.text: "rot, rot — roht."

Say "red." (Rot.) Is the o long or short? (Long — as in road.) Which colour do languages name third? (Red.) And the first two? (Dark and light — black and white.) Next: the cousin it has in French, and why it is not a borrowing.

lessons.title: rot, taken apart
lessons.gloss: one of the oldest colour words we can reconstruct — and rot and rouge are cousins, not borrowings

segments.text: The last lesson had a German word the Romance languages borrowed. This one has a German word they did not borrow — and they have it anyway.
Rot comes from Germanic raudaz, and behind that from Proto-Indo-European h₁rewdʰ- — one of the oldest colour words that can be reconstructed at all. It went everywhere:

utterances: language: German. what it became: rot.
language: English. what it became: red, and rust, ruddy.
language: Latin. what it became: ruber, rubeus — and so French rouge, plus ruby, rubric.

segments.text: So rot and rouge are cousins, not borrowings. They did not pass from one language to the other; they split apart thousands of years before either language existed, and each walked its own road to a word for red.
That is a different relationship from the one blank has with blanc. There, a word crossed a border within recorded history. Here, two words inherited the same ancestor and never met again.

segments.instruction: the two relationships — "blank and blanc: borrowed. Rot and rouge: cousins."
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two relationships — "blank and blanc: borrowed. Rot and rouge: cousins."]

segments.text: "rot, red, rouge."

Which French word is rot's relative? (Rouge.) Did French borrow it from German? (No — they are cousins.) Which Latin word is in the line? (Ruber.) Name two English words from the same root besides red. (Rust, ruddy.) Next: the fourth colour, which was borrowed.

lessons.title: blau — "blue"
lessons.gloss: blue — the fourth colour, and the second German word the Romance languages took

segments.text: The fourth and last colour of the set — and the second one German lent abroad.
blau — "blue."
Four letters, one syllable, and the vowel is the trap.
diphthong-au — German au is the vowel of English house or cow. It is not the aw of law and not the oo of blue.
So blau rhymes with English cow: blow as in plough, never blow as in blew.
That one vowel is what stops an English speaker recognising the word by ear even though it is the same word.

segments.instruction: the wrong one, then the right one — "not bloo … blau"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the wrong one, then the right one — "not *bloo* … *blau*"]
[YOU SAY: all four — "schwarz, weiß, rot, blau"]

segments.text: "blau, blau — rhymes with cow."

Say "blue." (Blau.) Which English word does it rhyme with? (Cow.) Does it rhyme with blue? (No.) Say all four colours. (Schwarz, weiß, rot, blau.) Next: the journey this word took, and the odd route English used to get it back.

lessons.title: blau, taken apart
lessons.gloss: the second Germanic emigrant — and English took the French form, so its blue came home in disguise

segments.text: Blank emigrated. So did this one — and then English did something strange to get it back.
Blau comes from Germanic blēwaz, and like blank before it, this word was borrowed into Romance:

utterances: language: English. "blue": blue — taken from French, not from Germanic.

segments.text: Read that last row twice. English is Germanic. It had inherited blēwaz itself — the word was already sitting in Old English — and it borrowed the French form anyway.

So the word went Germanic becomes French becomes English, and arrived home wearing Romance clothes. English blue is a German word that took the long way round and is no longer recognisable as one — which is exactly why blau does not sound like blue.

Portuguese went somewhere else entirely: its blue is azul, from Arabic. One colour, and within a few hundred miles you can find a Germanic word, a Germanic word laundered through French, and an Arabic one.
Colour words travel more than almost any other kind, because they are easy to borrow: you can point at the thing. Verbs and grammar stay home; the names of shades move with cloth, dye and trade.

segments.instruction: the long way round — "Germanic, French, English"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the long way round — "Germanic, French, English"]

segments.text: "blau, bleu, blue — one word, three stops."

Which two German colour words did Romance borrow? (Blank and blau.) Where did English get blue from? (French — not directly from Germanic.) Which language's blue is Arabic? (Portuguese — azul.) Next: all four colours, and what each of them did.

lessons.title: Practice — four colours, four histories
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — four colours, four different relationships with the neighbours

segments.text: No new words. Four colours, and no two of them got where they are the same way.

utterances: German: schwarz. source: Germanic swartaz. did Romance take it?: no.
German: weiß. source: Germanic hwītaz. did Romance take it?: no — but blank went instead.
German: rot. source: Germanic raudaz. did Romance take it?: no — Latin had its own cousin.
German: blau. source: Germanic blēwaz. did Romance take it?: yes — bleu, blu.

segments.text: Four native Germanic words and not a Latin borrowing among them, which is worth saying plainly: German did not get its colours from Rome. Two of them went the other way.

And the "no" in row three is a different kind of no from the ones above it. Schwarz and weiß stayed home. Rot has a Romance relative anyway — because Latin inherited the same ancient word rather than borrowing the German one.
